title: Optimizing Global Logistics Tracking
business: A global logistics provider managing millions of container transit records.
problem: As the transit history table grows, retrieving the status of a specific container using a unique identifier requires a full table scan, causing significant latency during peak operational hours.
solution: Implementing a B-tree index on the container identifier column creates a searchable structure that maps keys to stored records, allowing the database engine to locate specific rows without scanning the entire dataset.
steps: Analyze the query patterns to identify the column frequently used in WHERE clauses.
Execute the CREATE INDEX command targeting the unique container identifier column.
Verify the query execution plan to ensure the index is being utilized by the planner.
Monitor the impact on write operations to ensure the overhead remains within acceptable bounds.
outcome: The system achieves consistent lookup times for container status queries, regardless of the total volume of historical transit data stored in the table.
limitation: Indexes introduce a write-time penalty because every insert or update operation must also update the index structure; this can be checked by monitoring transaction commit latency during high-volume data ingestion.

questions.question: In Optimizing Global Logistics Tracking, what is the primary tradeoff of implementing an index?
options: It increases the storage size of the database indefinitely.
It requires a complete rewrite of all existing application queries.
It introduces a write-time penalty during data ingestion.
It makes the database unable to perform updates.
questions.explanation: Indexes must be updated whenever data changes, which adds overhead to write operations.
